prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes exporting and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B037 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler) and listed B048 as my first alternative. I now put B048 first. The reasons are specific. First, the exchange sharpened the attribution problem in B037. Hassler would credit only Kiyotaki and Moore, and Gertler's record is split with B040 and entangled with the Bernanke lineage recognised in 2022. I said I would accept a two-name version if Gertler's credit looked too entangled. Several colleagues have now made that argument. Second, the 2022 prize does not disqualify B037, but it reduces the marginal novelty of the credit-friction theme. Third, B037's strongest part is a mechanism whose quantitative empirical identification is harder than its influence suggests. B048 has none of these weaknesses to the same degree. Melitz (2003) is an identifiable originating model, and Helpman is the natural second name through the exporting-versus-FDI work and his earlier trade theory. The qualitative predictions (selection into exporting, exporter premia, within-industry reallocation after liberalisation) have been tested in firm-level data across many countries for over twenty years. Selection and reallocation are now organising ideas in macro, growth and development, which I see daily from the heterogeneous-agent side. As a macroeconomist I should not rate this candidate higher for that reason, but it is evidence the idea travels. It is distinct from the 2008 prize for new trade theory with representative firms, and I do not count the 2008 prize or field rotation as evidence against its merit. On the chair's question about priority, a citation limited to the selection and reallocation mechanism and the gains-from-trade framework is sufficient and honest. It does not overclaim the empirical firm-level facts. Head to head with B001, I prefer B048 if the citation must rest on tested findings. The research design and data behind B001 are a real contribution, but the central causal claim is the contested part and Vishny is excluded by the cap. I do not think B048 is a close call against B037 on the dimensions of attribution and robustness.
statement.case_against: The main risk is priority. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (and Yeaple) developed parallel firm-level facts and models, and none is on this ballot entry. A two-name credit therefore leaves out part of the empirical foundation. Welfare-gain magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, so the prize should rest on the qualitative mechanism and not on specific quantitative gains. Helpman also appears in another package (B026), which complicates how his credit is framed. A trade prize in 2008 may shape field balance, though that is not scientific evidence. I also acknowledge that I am a macroeconomist, so I may under-weight identification problems in trade that a trade specialist would stress. I left B037 because of attribution and overlap, not because its scientific merit is low, and a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize remains a mature and defensible outcome.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B037 third and would credit only Kiyotaki and Moore, since Gertler's accelerator and intermediary work overlaps with Bernanke (2022) and with his claim on B040. He ranks B001 slightly ahead of B048 because he finds field creation more decisive, and he calls the gap small.
responses.response: I accept his attribution argument on B037 and it is a main reason I moved. Kiyotaki and Moore are the clean core, and my case for adding Gertler depended on a distinction between the accelerator and later intermediary-based quantitative work. That distinction is real but it does not make the credit clean. Where I still differ is on B001 against B048. Field creation matters, but I weigh it below the stability of the central claim. You yourself would not want a citation that endorses the strong causal legal-origins reading. Once the citation is worded around measurable institutions and regularities, I think the tested core predictions of B048 and its cleaner two-name attribution outweigh the cost of the Vishny exclusion.

responses.point: Dreber prefers B048 and lists B037 as her first alternative. She finds the collateral-constraint mechanism cleanly attributable but harder to identify empirically than its influence suggests. She notes the financial-accelerator overlap with the 2022 prize and that Gertler's credit is split with the New Keynesian entry.
responses.response: I now agree with her ordering. My round-1 reply took the reservations seriously but kept B037 first. Having read the other files, I think the combination matters: a split credit for Gertler, overlap with 2022, and empirical identification that rests mostly on conceptual impact. Each is a manageable weakness alone, but together they make B037 less well supported than B048. I would still keep it as an alternative. I also agree that the B048 citation should be written around the selection mechanism, as she proposes.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B048 first. She calls the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question the real vulnerability, since it concerns the empirical foundations and not just a later extension. She proposes drafting the citation around the selection mechanism and the gains-from-trade framework.
responses.response: I agree that this is the vulnerability, and the three-name cap cannot fix it, because the people outside the entry are not a single strand. Her drafting solution is the right one. If the committee later decides the priority question is material, my fallback would be to prefer a different configuration, not to widen B048 with an arbitrary third name. I am not at that point. The mechanism and the extension to exporting versus FDI are carried by Melitz and Helpman, and the empirical firm-level facts were developed in parallel and supported the mechanism.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B001 first. He argues that the strongest lasting contribution is the cross-country facts and research design, not the causal legal-origins story, and he would word the citation accordingly. He says the critiques qualify the mechanism more than they undermine the discovery. He also says that in my round-1 file I raised replication and conduct concerns that he cannot assess.
responses.response: I accept that a prize can recognise the founding of a field even where its first causal story is only partly right, and I take his point that reputational concerns should not enter the merit case. I cannot assess them from the evidence supplied and I do not rely on them. My preference rests on a narrower comparison. His wording, centred on data and design, would be defensible, but it would then reward the empirical regularities and the agenda, while B048 rewards a mechanism that made specific predictions and survived testing. The Vishny exclusion also costs B001 more than the cap costs B048. I would not oppose B001 as an outcome, which is why I list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B037 seventh with Kiyotaki and Moore only, saying the mechanism is cleanly attributable but the 2022 prize may reduce the area's relative standing. He prefers B048 and, after discussion, dropped Redding.
responses.response: In round 1 I said the 2022 prize should not push B037 down to seventh, because it addressed banking and the origins of crises while Kiyotaki-Moore addresses amplification through collateral values. I still think that distinction holds, so I do not treat B037 as weak. But the overlap is real in the credit structure, and combined with the Gertler problem it is enough for me to move. I agree with his dropping Redding. His quantitative and spatial work is a later wave, and a third name would blur the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee considers the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question material enough to change the configuration. A two-name credit cannot accommodate those names.
How far the welfare-gain results depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and whether this weakens the claim of a robust discovery.
How Helpman's appearance in another package (B026) affects his claim here, and whether it is best handled by defining the citation tightly.

Whether the 2022 prize overlap and Gertler's split credit should have moved me off B037. A two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize remains defensible, and I may be over-weighting attribution tidiness relative to conceptual impact.

Whether B001's field-creating contribution should outrank B048's tested predictions if the citation rests on data and research design. My ordering rests on my own reading of the literature, which I have not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Melitz, Helpman, Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist, Shleifer, La Porta or Lopez-de-Silanes appears in my supplied profile. My long-term co-authors (Hassler, Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski, Olovsson) are not credited names on any part I propose or list as an alternative. I disclose co-authorship with committee colleagues Timo Boppart and John Hassler, and IIES ties to both. I serve as committee secretary. I am a macroeconomist working on heterogeneous-agent models, which is adjacent to the B037 candidate I moved away from and to the macro uses of heterogeneous-firm models, not to trade itself. I applied common criteria across fields and do not adjudicate these connections.
